title: Your Lease Ends in 12 Months: Should You Buy Office Furniture Now?
metaTitle: Buying Office Furniture Before Your Lease Ends | YOS
metaDescription: Decide whether to buy office furniture before lease expiry. Compare renewal, relocation and uncertain plans with a practical purchase decision checklist.
excerpt: A lease expiry changes the furniture brief. Decide what to buy now, what to keep flexible and what to defer until you know whether the business will renew or relocate.
body:
You can buy office furniture with 12 months left on a lease, but the decision should reflect whether you expect to renew, relocate or are still undecided. Address unsuitable or worn furniture when needed, favour purchases that can work in more than one layout, and defer expensive premises-specific items until the property plan is clearer.

Twelve months is a planning prompt, not a legal deadline or a universal procurement timeline. Your actual notice requirements, option dates and purchasing lead times may require action earlier. Check the signed lease and obtain appropriate advice on its terms.

## Start with the property decision

Before committing to a large furniture order, write down the most likely property outcome and what could change it. Is the current office still suitable for your team? Is renewal being investigated? Is a move likely because of growth, location or layout constraints?

A furniture refresh can improve an existing office, but it cannot resolve every premises problem. Equally, a possible move does not mean every furniture purchase should stop. Separate immediate needs from decisions that depend on the next floor plan.

[Compare renewing and relocating a commercial lease](/blog/renew-or-relocate-commercial-lease)

## Use this purchase decision table

| Property position | Reasonable purchases to assess now | Decisions to resolve first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Renewal is the preferred plan | Replacement seating, worn furniture and a measured refresh of the existing layout | Renewal position, future headcount and whether the layout needs building work |
| Relocation is likely | Furniture with dimensions and components suitable for multiple layouts | Shortlisted floor plans, access routes, retained inventory and moving costs |
| The outcome is uncertain | Targeted replacements and flexible items with a clear current use | What can wait, how much temporary change is justified and when the property decision will be made |

These are assessment prompts, not automatic recommendations. A standard desk can still be wrong for the next workplace, and a bespoke item can be justified if it serves a confirmed brief.

## If you expect to renew, test the workplace before refreshing it

Confirm what the team needs over the next occupation period. Look at actual attendance, desk use, meeting requirements, storage and planned growth. Ask staff which furniture problems affect their work rather than selecting replacements solely from photographs.

Compare a furniture-only refresh with any wider works required to make the layout function. Moving desks may also require changes to power, data or circulation. Confirm the appropriate building approvals and qualified trade scope before treating a rearrangement as a simple furniture job.

Check the lease renewal process separately. A preferred outcome is not the same as a secured renewal. Avoid basing a major location-specific purchase on an assumption that the business can stay.

## If you expect to relocate, inventory before you order

Record existing furniture by quantity, dimensions, condition and product code where available. Photograph workstation connections, screens and accessories. Identify what can be dismantled and who should reassemble it.

Test that inventory against a measured plan of each serious premises option. Consider room proportions, circulation, storage and how people use the office. A desk that fits on paper may create an impractical layout when equipment, chairs and movement are included.

Check the entire access route as well as the room. A retained boardroom table is only useful if it can be transported, brought into the new building and installed at a reasonable cost.

[Assess furniture that can move and grow with the business](/blog/adaptable-office-furniture-growth-relocation)

## If you are undecided, separate three purchasing categories

### Buy when there is a justified immediate need

Assess damaged, unsuitable or insufficient furniture promptly. Do not delay addressing a workplace problem solely because the lease may end. Choose the response appropriate to the actual issue, including repair or replacement where suitable.

### Keep flexible when the next layout is unknown

Consider items with dimensions, dismantling requirements and components that can suit more than one realistic layout. Confirm product compatibility and current availability. Modular branding alone does not establish that a system can be expanded or divided later.

### Defer when the item depends on the premises

Large built-in settings, room-specific reception pieces and complex workstation configurations can be difficult to justify before the next layout is confirmed. Ask whether the purchase is removable, what alterations are needed and whether it makes sense if you move.

## Worked scenario: replacing seating without committing to a new layout

Consider a fictional business with 20 staff, several worn chairs and no confirmed decision about renewing its lease. The immediate issue is seating; the unresolved issue is the future office layout.

One option is to trial and replace the unsuitable chairs now, document the selected products and assess how they can move later. The business can then defer a large joined workstation order until it has a measured layout and a clearer property decision.

That approach is not automatically cheaper. The business still needs quotes for repair, replacement, delivery and moving, plus a review of chair suitability. Its value is that it separates an immediate workplace need from a purchase dependent on unknown premises.

## Compare the cost of buying twice

For each proposed item, compare buying now and moving it with buying after the property decision. Include any interim repair or replacement needed if you wait.

| Cost or requirement | Question to answer |
| --- | --- |
| Purchase and current installation | What is needed to make the item usable now? |
| Later dismantling and moving | Can it be moved, by whom and at what quoted cost? |
| Reinstallation and alterations | Does the next layout require new components or trade work? |
| Storage or duplicated furniture | What happens during any gap or overlap between premises? |
| Removal and handback | What does the signed lease require for your existing premises? |
| Deferred purchase | What immediate need remains unresolved, and what interim response is appropriate? |

Use actual quotes and label unknowns. Do not assume that reuse is free, that every piece will fit or that waiting has no operational cost.

[Compare the real installed cost of furniture quotes](/blog/compare-office-furniture-quotes-installed-cost)

## Coordinate the lease, FitOut and furniture program

Check option dates, notice requirements and handback obligations against the signed lease. Ask your solicitor to explain the applicable terms. NSW retail and other commercial leases can operate under different rules; general retail tenancy guidance should not be treated as a universal office lease rule.

Set your project sequence around confirmed requirements: property decision, measured workplace brief, necessary approvals, furniture specifications, procurement, installation and handover. Work back from your intended operating date using supplier-confirmed lead times and site requirements.

## Use the lease-to-furniture decision checklist

Record the property outcome, immediate needs, reusable inventory, unresolved measurements and decisions that can wait. Assign a person and decision date to each outstanding item. Use the date required by your lease or project program rather than relying on a generic 12-month timetable.

[Open or save the lease-to-furniture decision checklist](/downloads/lease-to-furniture-decision-checklist.txt)

## Frequently asked questions

### Should we wait until the new lease is signed to buy furniture?

Not for every item. Assess immediate needs and whether a purchase remains suitable across realistic outcomes. Confirm the property and layout before committing to expensive premises-specific furniture.

### Is 12 months before expiry the correct time to start?

It is a useful planning prompt, not a fixed rule. Lease option windows, approvals, supplier lead times and project complexity determine your actual program and can require earlier action.

### Can we take existing workstations to another office?

Possibly. Check ownership, condition, dimensions, dismantling requirements, access and compatibility with the new layout. Obtain moving and installation quotes before relying on reuse.

### Will furniture purchases reduce our make-good obligations?

Do not assume so. Removal and reinstatement obligations depend on your lease, alterations and any agreed arrangements. Have the relevant terms reviewed before planning handback.

## Further reading

The NSW Small Business Commissioner explains that tenants should check how and when a lease option must be exercised. Its guidance also distinguishes retail and commercial leasing frameworks. These resources support the lease review; they do not replace advice on your signed office lease.
